questions.question: Who has the power to appoint the Chief Minister (CM) of a state in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Governor of the State**__.

**__Key Points__**

• According to **Article 164** of the **Constitution of India**, the **Chief Minister** shall be appointed by the **Governor**. This is the standard constitutional procedure followed in the **parliamentary system** of government at the state level. ***Hence, the correct answer is Governor of the State.***

• The **Governor** does not have the freedom to appoint anyone as the **Chief Minister**; they must appoint the leader of the party or coalition that commands a **majority** in the **State Legislative Assembly** (Vidhan Sabha).

• The **President of India** is responsible for appointing the **Prime Minister** under **Article 75** and the **Governors** of states under **Article 155**, but they do not directly appoint the **Chief Minister** of a state. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The **Prime Minister** is the head of the **Union Government** and while they may have political influence over the selection of a candidate within their party, they do not possess the **legal or constitutional power** to appoint a **Chief Minister**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***

questions.question: In 2024, Smt. Vijaya Kishore Rahatkar was appointed as the 9th Chairperson of the National Commission for Women (NCW). Which of the following is **correct** regarding her role and responsibilities?

options.text: Designing fiscal and tax policies for women's entrepreneurship
Framing monetary policies for women's economic development
Reviewing legal safeguards for women and recommending remedial measures
Conducting national elections and preparing voter lists

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Reviewing legal safeguards for women and recommending remedial measures**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• Smt. **Vijaya Kishore Rahatkar** was appointed as the **9th Chairperson** of the **National Commission for Women (NCW)** in **October 2024**.

• The **National Commission for Women** is a **statutory body** formed under the **National Commission for Women Act, 1990**, to protect and promote the interests of women in India.

• The core responsibility of the NCW and its Chairperson is to **review the constitutional and legal safeguards** provided for women and recommend **remedial legislative measures** to address any gaps or inadequacies.

• The Commission is empowered to **investigate and examine** all matters relating to the safeguards provided for women under the Constitution and other laws.

• It also takes **suo motu notice** of matters involving the deprivation of women's rights and non-implementation of laws enacted to provide protection to women.

• **Option 1 and 2** are incorrect because **fiscal, tax, and monetary policies** fall under the jurisdiction of the **Ministry of Finance** and the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**.

• **Option 4** is incorrect as the **Election Commission of India** is responsible for conducting national elections and preparing voter lists.

**Additional Information__**

• The **NCW** was established on **31st January 1992**. The first Chairperson of the commission was **Jayanti Patnaik**.

• Smt. **Vijaya Rahatkar** has a significant background in public service, having served as the Chairperson of the **Maharashtra State Commission for Women** (2016-2021) and the Mayor of **Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad)**.

• The Commission consists of a **Chairperson**, five members (with at least one member each from **Scheduled Castes** and **Scheduled Tribes**), and a **Member Secretary**.

• The NCW also participates and advises on the **planning process** of socio-economic development of women and evaluates the progress of the development of women under the Union and any State.
</ul

questions.question:
Fill in the blank:
The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam modernizes _______ by incorporating provisions for technology-based evidence.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Evidence laws**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023** (BSA) was enacted to replace the **Indian Evidence Act, 1872**, marking a significant shift in India's legal framework regarding the admissibility of proof.

• The primary purpose of this legislation is to modernize **evidence laws** by incorporating comprehensive provisions for **technology-based evidence**.

• Under the BSA, the definition of **documents** has been expanded to include **electronic and digital records**, such as emails, server logs, documents on computers, smartphones, and even messages sent via communication platforms.

• It establishes that **digital evidence** shall have the same legal effect, validity, and enforceability as paper records, thereby facilitating a more efficient judicial process in the digital era.

• Other options like **Civil laws**, **Consumer laws**, and **Tax laws** are incorrect because they refer to substantive or procedural laws governed by different statutes like the Code of Civil Procedure, Consumer Protection Act, and Income Tax Act, rather than the rules of evidence.

**Additional Information__**

• The **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam** is one of the three major criminal law reforms passed by the Indian Parliament in **December 2023**.

• The other two laws in this reform package are the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (replacing the Indian Penal Code) and the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** (replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure).

• The act received **Presidential assent** on **December 25, 2023**, and aims to remove colonial-era terminology and align the justice system with contemporary technological realities.

• It allows for the **oral evidence** to be given electronically, enabling witnesses, accused persons, and victims to appear via **audio-video means**.
</ul

questions.question: Which recent ISRO mission aims to explore the Sun-Earth Lagrange Point (L1)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aditya-L1**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• **Aditya-L1** is the first dedicated **Indian space mission** designed to observe and study the **Sun** from a **halo orbit**.

• The mission is positioned at the **Lagrange Point 1 (L1)** of the **Sun-Earth system**, which is located about **1.5 million kilometers** away from Earth.

• The primary advantage of placing a spacecraft at the **L1 point** is that it allows for a continuous, unobstructed view of the **Sun** without any **occultation** or **eclipses**.

• **Chandrayaan-4** is a planned future mission by **ISRO** intended for **lunar sample return**, following the success of Chandrayaan-3.

• **Mangalyaan-2**, also known as **Mars Orbiter Mission 2 (MOM 2)**, is a proposed second mission to **Mars** to study its surface and atmosphere.

• **Astrosat-2** is envisioned as a successor to **Astrosat**, India's first dedicated multi-wavelength **space observatory**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The **Aditya-L1** mission was successfully launched on **September 2, 2023**, from the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** in Sriharikota using the **PSLV-C57** rocket.

• The spacecraft carries **seven scientific payloads**, including the **Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC)** and the **Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT)**.

• The mission objectives include studying **coronal heating**, **solar wind acceleration**, **coronal mass ejections (CMEs)**, and the dynamics of the **solar atmosphere**.

• **Lagrange Points** are specific positions in space where the gravitational forces of two large bodies (like the Sun and Earth) produce enhanced regions of attraction and repulsion, allowing a spacecraft to maintain a **stable position** with minimal fuel consumption.
</ul

questions.question:
Fill in the blank:
The National Digital Health Mission's (NDHM) primary aim is to create a unique ________ for every Indian citizen.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Health ID**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **National Digital Health Mission (NDHM)**, now known as the **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM)**, was launched by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** on **August 15, 2020**.

• The primary aim of the mission is to provide a **Health ID** (now referred to as **ABHA - Ayushman Bharat Health Account**) to every Indian citizen to digitize their health records.

• The **Health ID** serves as a repository for all health-related information, including **medical history**, **prescriptions**, **diagnostic reports**, and **discharge summaries**, ensuring seamless access to healthcare services across the country.

• **Vaccine ID** is a specific identifier for immunization status and is not the overarching goal of the NDHM.

• **Aadhaar ID** is a 12-digit unique identity number for residents of India for general identification, while the Health ID is specifically designed for the **healthcare ecosystem**.

• A **Disease Registry** is a database that collects information about individuals diagnosed with a specific condition, which is a component of the health system but not the primary identification tool for every citizen.

**Additional Information__**

• The **National Health Authority (NHA)** is the implementing agency for the **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission**.

• The **ABHA number** is a **14-digit** unique identification number that can be generated using an **Aadhaar card** or a **mobile number**.

• The mission also includes the **Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR)** and **Health Facility Registry (HFR)** to bring all stakeholders (doctors, hospitals, and labs) onto a single digital platform.

• It promotes **interoperability** within the digital health ecosystem, allowing patients to share their health profiles with doctors and insurance providers digitally with their **informed consent**.
</ul

questions.question: Which principle explains how rockets are propelled forward when fuel is ejected in the opposite direction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Newton's Third Law of Motion**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Newton's Third Law of Motion** states that for every **action**, there is an **equal and opposite reaction**. This is the fundamental principle that explains how a rocket moves.

• In a rocket engine, fuel is burned to produce high-pressure **exhaust gases**. These gases are expelled out of the back of the rocket at very high velocities. This downward or backward flow of gas is the **action**.

• The **reaction** to this action is an upward or forward force, called **thrust**, exerted by the gases on the rocket, which propels it forward.

• **Newton's First Law of Motion** (Law of Inertia) states that an object will remain at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force. While it explains why a rocket needs a force to move, it doesn't explain the mechanism of propulsion itself.

• The **Law of Conservation of Mass** states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. While mass is conserved as fuel turns into gas, it does not explain the movement.

• The **Law of Gravitation** explains the force of attraction between two masses (like the Earth and the rocket). This force actually pulls the rocket back toward Earth and must be overcome by the rocket's thrust.

**Additional Information__**

• Rocket propulsion is also deeply rooted in the **Law of Conservation of Momentum**. The momentum gained by the expelled exhaust gases in one direction is exactly balanced by the momentum gained by the rocket in the opposite direction.

• Rockets are unique because they carry both **fuel** and an **oxidizer**. This allows them to function in the **vacuum of space**, where there is no oxygen to support combustion and no air to push against.

• The speed a rocket reaches depends on the velocity of the exhaust gases and the ratio of the rocket's initial mass to its final mass (after the fuel is spent), a relationship known as the **Tsiolkovsky rocket equation**.

• Common examples of **Newton's Third Law** in daily life include **recoil of a gun** when a bullet is fired and the movement of a **swimmer** pushing against water to move forward.
</ul

questions.question: Which Union Territory has the lowest population in India in reference to the Census 2011?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lakshadweep**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• According to the **Census 2011**, **Lakshadweep** is the Union Territory with the **lowest population** in **India**. The total population of this archipelago was recorded as **64,473** individuals. *Hence, the option is correct.*

• **Andaman & Nicobar Islands** had a population of **380,581** as per the **2011** data, which is significantly higher than that of **Lakshadweep**. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

• **Puducherry** recorded a population of **1,247,953**, making it one of the more populous Union Territories in the country. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

• **Ladakh** was not a separate Union Territory during the **Census 2011**; it was part of the state of **Jammu and Kashmir**. It only became a Union Territory on **31 October 2019** following the **Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019**. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

• **Lakshadweep** is also the smallest Union Territory in **India** in terms of **land area**, covering only **32 sq km**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Census 2011** was the **15th National Census** of **India** and the **7th** census conducted after **Independence**. It was carried out under the guidance of **C. Chandramouli**, who served as the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner** of **India**.

• **Uttar Pradesh** is the most populous state in **India**, with a population of approximately **19.98 crore**, while **Sikkim** is the least populous state with a population of **6.10 lakh**.

• Among all the Union Territories, the **National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi** has the highest population, recorded at **1.67 crore** in the **2011** survey.

• The total population of **India** as per the **2011 Census** was **1,210,854,977** (approximately **1.21 billion**), which accounted for about **17.5%** of the world population at that time.

• The **decadal growth rate** of the Indian population during the period **2001-2011** was **17.7%**, showing a slight decrease compared to the previous decade.

**Important Points__**

• **Lakshadweep** is a group of **36 islands** located in the **Arabian Sea**, though only **10** of these islands are inhabited by humans. The capital of this Union Territory is **Kavaratti**.

• The **literacy rate** in **Lakshadweep** is exceptionally high at **91.85%**, which is one of the highest in **India**, surpassed only by **Kerala** among states.

• The **sex ratio** in **Lakshadweep** according to the **2011 Census** is **946** females per **1000** males, which is better than the national average of **943**.

• The **population density** of **Lakshadweep** is **2,149** persons per **sq km**, reflecting a high concentration of people on its limited landmass.

• The main languages spoken in the territory are **Malayalam** and **Mahl**, with the latter being predominantly spoken on **Minicoy Island**.
</ul

questions.question: The Partition of Bengal in 1905 was carried out under which Viceroy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Curzon**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Partition of Bengal** was carried out in **1905** by **Lord Curzon**, who served as the **Viceroy of India** from **1899 to 1905**. This decision is considered one of the most controversial acts of his tenure. ***Hence, the statement regarding Lord Curzon is correct.***

• The partition was officially announced on **July 19, 1905**, and it was formally implemented on **October 16, 1905**. The British government claimed that the **Bengal Presidency**, which included **Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha**, was too large (with a population of nearly **80 million**) to be administered efficiently.

• The real political motive behind the partition was to weaken the **Indian National Movement**, which was centered in **Bengal**. By dividing the province, the British aimed to create a communal rift between the **Hindu-majority West Bengal** and the **Muslim-majority East Bengal and Assam**.

• **Lord Ripon (1880-1884)** was known for the **Ilbert Bill** and the **repeal of the Vernacular Press Act**. He is often called the **Father of Local Self-Government** in India. He was not associated with the 1905 partition. ***Hence, the option Lord Ripon is incorrect.***

• **Lord Lytton (1876-1880)** is remembered for the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, the **Arms Act (1878)**, and the **Second Anglo-Afghan War**. His term ended long before the partition occurred. ***Hence, the option Lord Lytton is incorrect.***

• **Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856)** is famous for the **Doctrine of Lapse**, the introduction of the **Railways (1853)**, and the **Post and Telegraph** system. He left India nearly half a century before the partition. ***Hence, the option Lord Dalhousie is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Swadeshi Movement:** The partition triggered the **Swadeshi Movement**, which focused on the **boycott of British goods** and the promotion of **Indian-made products**. Leaders like **Surendranath Banerjee**, **Bipin Chandra Pal**, and **Lala Lajpat Rai** played a pivotal role in this mass agitation.

• **Annulment of Partition:** Due to relentless protests and the rise of revolutionary activities, the **Partition of Bengal** was finally **annulled in 1911** by **Lord Hardinge II** during the **Delhi Durbar**.

• **Capital Shift:** In the same year (**1911**), the British government decided to shift the **capital of India** from **Calcutta** to **Delhi** to ensure better administrative control and to appease the sentiments of the people.

• **Cultural Impact:** **Rabindranath Tagore** composed the song **'Amar Sonar Bangla'** (now the national anthem of Bangladesh) as a mark of protest. He also encouraged people to tie **Rakhi** on each other's wrists as a symbol of **Hindu-Muslim unity** on the day the partition came into effect.

• **Formation of Muslim League:** One of the long-term consequences of the communal divide fostered by the partition was the formation of the **All India Muslim League** in **1906** at **Dacca** (now Dhaka) under the leadership of **Nawab Salimullah**.

**Important Points__**

• **Administrative Reforms of Curzon:** Apart from the partition, **Lord Curzon** is known for the **Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904)**, the establishment of the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)**, and the **Indian Universities Act (1904)**.

• **Surat Split (1907):** The difference in opinion regarding the methods of the **Anti-Partition Movement** (Moderates vs. Extremists) eventually led to the **Surat Split** of the **Indian National Congress** in **1907**.

• **Geographical Division:** The **Eastern Province** included **Assam** and the districts of **Dacca, Rajshahi, and Chittagong**, with its capital at **Dacca**. The **Western Province** included **Bihar and Orissa**, with its capital at **Calcutta**.
</ul

questions.question: The Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883 was related to which issue?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rights of Indian judges**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Ilbert Bill** was a legislative measure introduced in **1883** during the viceroyalty of **Lord Ripon**. It was drafted by **Sir Courtenay Peregrine Ilbert**, who was the **Legal Member** of the **Viceroy's Executive Council**.

• The primary objective of the bill was to address the issue of **judicial disqualification** based on race. Before this bill, according to the **Criminal Procedure Code of 1873**, **Indian judges** and **magistrates** in the interior (mofussil) were not allowed to try **European British subjects** in criminal cases, even if the Indian judge was senior in rank.

• The bill proposed to grant **Indian District Magistrates** and **Sessions Judges** the same jurisdiction and **Rights of Indian judges** as their European counterparts to try Europeans. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*

• The bill did not deal with the **Introduction of income tax**. Income tax in **India** was first introduced in **1860** by **James Wilson** to overcome the financial difficulties caused by the **Revolt of 1857**. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*

• The **Expansion of railways** was a process that began much earlier, with the first train running between **Bombay** and **Thane** in **1853** under **Lord Dalhousie**. The **Ilbert Bill** had no relation to railway infrastructure. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.*

• The **Indianisation of the army** was a political demand that gained significant momentum during the **20th century**, particularly after **World War I**, and was not the subject of the **1883** controversy. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Lord Ripon**, who served as **Viceroy** from **1880** to **1884**, is regarded as one of the most liberal administrators in **British India**. He is known for the **Repeal of the Vernacular Press Act (1882)** and the **Resolution on Local Self-Government (1882)**.

• The **European community** in **India**, especially the **indigo and tea planters** in **Bengal**, reacted with extreme hostility to the bill. They viewed it as an insult to their racial superiority and formed the **European and Anglo-Indian Defence Association** to protest against it.

• This organized resistance by the British settlers is often referred to as the **White Mutiny**. They raised a fund of over **1.5 lakh rupees** and lobbied the government in **London** to withdraw the bill.

• Due to the intense pressure, a **compromise** was reached in **January 1884**. The amended bill allowed **Indian judges** to try Europeans, but the accused were given the right to demand a **jury**, of which at least **50%** of the members had to be **Europeans or Americans**.

• The **Ilbert Bill controversy** acted as a major catalyst for **Indian Nationalism**. It demonstrated to the **Indian intelligentsia** that they would never receive equal treatment under **British rule** without a unified political struggle.

**Important Points__**

• The controversy highlighted the **institutionalized racism** inherent in the **British colonial administration**. Even liberal reforms were thwarted by the collective pressure of the ruling race.

• **Surendranath Banerjee** and the **Indian National Association** (founded in **1876**) played a pivotal role in organizing counter-protests and support for the bill, which helped in the **political awakening** of the Indian middle class.

• The lessons learned from the **Ilbert Bill** agitation directly contributed to the formation of the **Indian National Congress** in **December 1885** at **Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College** in **Bombay**.

• The **compromise of 1884** was seen as a defeat for **Lord Ripon**, who eventually resigned from his post and returned to **England**, though he remained a hero to the **Indian people** for his efforts toward equality.
</ul

questions.question: The Baul music tradition belongs to which state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**West Bengal**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Baul** music is a unique and highly celebrated folk tradition that belongs to the state of **West Bengal** in **India** and the country of **Bangladesh**. It is not just a musical genre but a spiritual way of life practiced by a group of mystic minstrels known as **Bauls**.

• The tradition was recognized by **UNESCO** in **2005** when it was proclaimed a **Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity**, and it was later inscribed on the **Representative List** in **2008**.

• **Rajasthan** is incorrect because its folk music is primarily characterized by the **Manganiyar** and **Langa** traditions, which use instruments like the **Kamaicha** and **Khartal**.

• **Gujarat** is incorrect because it is famous for folk forms like **Garba**, **Dandiya Raas**, and **Siddhi Dhamal**, which are distinct from the mystic wandering tradition of the **Bauls**.

• **Tamil Nadu** is incorrect as it is the primary seat of **Carnatic Music** and folk forms such as **Karakattam** and **Villu Paatu**, which have different rhythmic and melodic structures compared to **Bengali** folk music.

• The **Baul** philosophy emphasizes the search for the divine within the human body, a concept known as **Moner Manush** (the Man of the Heart). They reject the caste system and formal religious rituals of both **Hinduism** and **Islam**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Lalon Shah** (also known as **Lalon Fakir**), who lived in the **19th century**, is the most iconic figure in the **Baul** tradition. His songs, which number in the thousands, form the core of the **Baul** repertoire and focus on social equality and spiritual liberation.

• The **Baul** tradition is a syncretic blend of **Sufism**, **Vaishnavism**, and **Sahajiya Buddhism**. This fusion allows **Bauls** to bridge the gap between different religious communities in **West Bengal**.

• **Rabindranath Tagore**, the **Nobel Prize** winner for Literature, was deeply influenced by **Baul** music. He incorporated its simple yet profound melodies and philosophical themes into his own compositions, known as **Rabindra Sangeet**.

• The **Poush Mela**, held annually in **Shantiniketan** in the **Birbhum** district of **West Bengal**, is a major cultural event where **Baul** singers from across the region gather to perform. Another significant gathering is the **Joydev Kenduli Mela**, held during **Makar Sankranti**.

• The instruments used in **Baul** music are simple and portable, reflecting their nomadic lifestyle. These include the **Ektara** (one-stringed lute), **Duggi** (a small hand drum), **Khol** (terracotta drum), and **Ghungur** (ankle bells worn by the singer while dancing).

**Important Points__**

• The word **Baul** is believed to be derived from the **Sanskrit** words **Vatula** (meaning mad or possessed by the wind) or **Vyakula** (meaning restless or impatient), signifying their intense spiritual longing.

• **Bauls** are easily identified by their distinctive attire, which often consists of a long, saffron or multi-colored patchwork robe called an **Alkhalla**, and they often keep long, matted hair.

• The lyrics of **Baul** songs are composed in the **Bengali** language and are famous for their use of **Sandhya Bhasha** (twilight language), which uses metaphors related to daily life, such as fishing or farming, to explain complex spiritual truths.

• Geographically, the heartland of the **Baul** tradition in **India** includes districts like **Birbhum**, **Nadia**, **Bankura**, and **Murshidabad** in **West Bengal**.
</ul

questions.question: The Jnanpith Award is given to authors for excellence in literature. Which author is NOT a recipient of the Jnanpith Award?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**R.K. Narayan**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **R.K. Narayan** (Rasipuram Krishnaswami Iyer Narayanaswami) was one of the most celebrated Indian novelists writing in **English**, famous for creating the fictional town of **Malgudi**. Although he received the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in **1960** for his novel **The Guide**, the **Padma Bhushan** in **1964**, and the **Padma Vibhushan** in **2001**, he was never a recipient of the **Jnanpith Award**. ***Hence, this option is correct.***

• **Gulzar**, the legendary **Urdu** poet, lyricist, and filmmaker, was conferred the **58th Jnanpith Award** for the year **2023**. He has previously received the **Sahitya Akademi Award** (2002), the **Padma Bhushan** (2004), and an **Academy Award**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

• **Jagadguru Rambhadracharya** is a renowned **Sanskrit** scholar, polyglot, and spiritual leader who has authored more than **100 books**. He was awarded the **58th Jnanpith Award** in **2023** alongside **Gulzar** for his immense contribution to **Sanskrit** literature. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***

• **Vinod Kumar Shukla** is a distinguished **Hindi** novelist and poet known for works like **Naukar Ki Kameez**. While he won the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in **1999** and the **PEN/Nabokov Award for Achievement in International Literature** in **2023**, he is not a **Jnanpith** laureate. However, in the context of standard literary assessments, **R.K. Narayan** remains the most prominent historical figure to have never received the award. ***Hence, this option is correct.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Jnanpith Award** is the **highest literary honor** in **India**, established in **1961** by the **Bharatiya Jnanpith**, a research and cultural institute founded by the **Sahu Jain family**.

• The award is presented annually to an **Indian citizen** for their **outstanding contribution towards literature**. Since **2013**, the award has also considered works written in the **English** language, alongside the **22 languages** listed in the **Eighth Schedule** of the **Constitution of India**.

• The first recipient of the **Jnanpith Award** was **G. Sankara Kurup** in **1965**, who won it for his collection of poems titled **Odakkuzhal** (The Bamboo Flute) in the **Malayalam** language.

• The prize includes a cash award of **Rs. 11 lakh**, a citation plaque, and a bronze replica of **Vagdevi** (Saraswati), the goddess of learning.

• The **57th Jnanpith Award** was presented to **Damodar Mauzo**, a **Konkani** novelist and short story writer, in **2022**.

**Important Points__**

• **Ashapoorna Devi** was the **first woman** to receive the **Jnanpith Award** in **1976** for her **Bengali** novel **Pratham Pratishruti**.

• **Amitav Ghosh** became the **first author** to be honored with the **Jnanpith Award** for literature in the **English** language in **2018**.

• The **58th Jnanpith Award** (announced in **2024** for the year **2023**) marked only the **second time** the award was given for the **Sanskrit** language and the **fifth time** for the **Urdu** language.

• **R.K. Narayan** is often grouped with **Mulk Raj Anand** and **Raja Rao** as the **trinity of Indian English literature**, yet none of these three pioneers received the **Jnanpith Award**, as it was not open to **English** writers during their primary active years.
</ul

questions.question: The Indian Olympic Association was formed in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1927**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Indian Olympic Association (IOA)** was established in the year **1927**. It is the apex body responsible for the **Olympic Movement** and the **Commonwealth Games** in **India**.

• The organization was founded by **Sir Dorabji Tata** and **Dr. A.G. Noehren**. **Sir Dorabji Tata** served as the **first President**, while **Dr. A.G. Noehren** was the **first Secretary General**.

• In **1927**, the **International Olympic Committee (IOC)** officially recognized the **Indian Olympic Association** as the **National Olympic Committee** for **India**.

• The formation of the **IOA** was a pivotal moment in formalizing **India's** participation in international multi-sport events, ensuring a structured approach to athlete selection and training.

• Regarding the other options: **1920** is the year **India** sent its first organized team to the **Antwerp Olympics**, but the **IOA** was not yet formed. **1930** marks the year of the first **British Empire Games** (now **Commonwealth Games**). **1947** is the year of **Indian Independence**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **First Participation:** **India** first participated in the **Olympic Games** in **1900** at the **Paris Olympics**. The country was represented by a lone athlete, **Norman Pritchard**, who won **two silver medals** in athletics (**200m** and **200m hurdles**).

• **Headquarters:** The headquarters of the **Indian Olympic Association** is located in **New Delhi**. It operates as a **Non-Profit Organization** registered under the **Societies Registration Act of 1860**.

• **Leadership:** In **December 2022**, the legendary sprinter **P.T. Usha** was elected as the **first woman President** of the **Indian Olympic Association**. She is also the first Olympian to lead the body.

• **Functions:** The **IOA** is responsible for managing the **Indian** contingents for the **Summer Olympics**, **Winter Olympics**, **Asian Games**, and **Commonwealth Games**. It also coordinates with various **National Sports Federations (NSFs)**.

• **Affiliations:** The **IOA** is a member of the **International Olympic Committee (IOC)**, the **Olympic Council of Asia (OCA)**, and the **Commonwealth Games Federation (CGF)**.

**Important Points__**

• **Early Efforts:** Before the formal establishment in **1927**, **Sir Dorabji Tata** personally financed the **Indian** team for the **1920 Antwerp Olympics**. A provisional **All-India Olympic Committee** was set up in **1923** to handle the **1924 Paris Olympics**.

• **Legal Status:** The **IOA** is governed by the **Olympic Charter** and its own constitution. It works closely with the **Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports**, **Government of India**, although it maintains its autonomy as a **National Olympic Committee**.

• **Role in Sports Development:** Beyond event management, the **IOA** plays a crucial role in promoting the **Olympic values** of **friendship**, **solidarity**, and **fair play** across the **country**.
</ul

questions.question: Which Indo-French structure is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Basilica of Bom Jesus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Basilica of Bom Jesus** is a renowned religious structure located in **Old Goa**, which was the former capital of **Portuguese India**.
 
• It is part of the **Churches and Convents of Goa**, which was declared a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **1986**. ***Hence, the statement regarding its UNESCO status is correct.***
 
• Construction of the basilica began in **1594** and was consecrated in **May 1605**. It stands as a landmark in the history of **Christianity** in **India**.
 
• The church is world-famous for housing the **mortal remains** of **St. Francis Xavier**, a co-founder of the **Society of Jesus** (Jesuits). The body is kept in a silver casket and is brought down for public viewing every **ten years**.
 
• Architecturally, it is one of the finest examples of **Baroque architecture** and **Manueline style** in **India**. It is the only church in **Goa** not covered with plaster on the outside, showcasing its **laterite** exterior.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fort St. George:**
 
 
• Located in **Chennai** (formerly Madras), **Fort St. George** was the first **English** (British) fortress in **India**, founded in **1644**.
 
• It currently serves as the headquarters of the **Legislative Assembly** of **Tamil Nadu**. While historically significant, it is **not** a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Auroville Matrimandir:**
 
 
• The **Matrimandir** is situated in the center of **Auroville**, an experimental township in **Puducherry** (and parts of Tamil Nadu).
 
• It was designed by the **French architect Roger Anger** and is a symbol of **integral yoga** and human unity. Although **French** in its architectural origin, it does not hold the **UNESCO World Heritage** status. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Chandannagar Strand:**
 
 
• **Chandannagar** was a former **French colony** located in **West Bengal**. The **Strand** is a beautiful promenade along the **Hooghly River**, lined with **French colonial** buildings.
 
• Despite its deep **Indo-French** cultural roots and heritage value, it has not been inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India:**
 
 
• As of **2024**, **India** has **42** designated **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**, which include **34 cultural**, **7 natural**, and **1 mixed** site.
 
• The **Churches and Convents of Goa** (including the **Basilica of Bom Jesus** and **Se Cathedral**) are protected under the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)**.
 
• The criteria for **UNESCO** inclusion for the **Goa** sites included their influence on the spread of **Manueline**, **Mannerist**, and **Baroque** art forms throughout **Asia**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The term **"Indo-French"** in the question likely refers to the European colonial influence on Indian architecture. However, strictly speaking, the **Basilica of Bom Jesus** is of **Portuguese** origin, while **Auroville** and **Chandannagar** are the primary **French** heritage sites in **India**.
 
• The **Basilica** was elevated to the status of a **Minor Basilica** in **1946**, the first in **India** to receive such an honor.
 
• The interior of the church is highly decorated with **gilded altars** and carvings, contrasting with its simple, unplastered **red laterite** exterior.
</ul
